recordings.transcript: Vercingetorix has done what no Gaul managed before: united tribes that spent generations raiding each other, then refused to fight Rome in the open. He burns his own countryside instead, starving the legions out of a land they cannot forage. When a cavalry engagement goes wrong he withdraws to Alesia, a hill fort of the Mandubii, with eighty thousand men. He expects to be besieged. He has already sent riders to every tribe in Gaul.

chunks.text: Vercingetorix has done what no Gaul managed before: united tribes that spent generations raiding each other, then refused to fight Rome in the open.
He burns his own countryside instead, starving the legions out of a land they cannot forage.
When a cavalry engagement goes wrong he withdraws to Alesia, a hill fort of the Mandubii, with eighty thousand men.
He expects to be besieged.
He has already sent riders to every tribe in Gaul.

recordings.transcript: Caesar does not assault the hill. He encircles it. Rampart, ditch and timber tower, built while under attack. In front of it: trenches, a channel flooded from the rivers, rows of sharpened branches, pits with fire-hardened stakes at the bottom, iron hooks set in blocks and buried in the ground. The legionaries called the pits lilies. These are not soldiers who can dig. They are engineers who happen to fight.

He encircles it.
Rampart, ditch and timber tower, built while under attack.
In front of it: trenches, a channel flooded from the rivers, rows of sharpened branches, pits with fire-hardened stakes at the bottom, iron hooks set in blocks and buried in the ground.
The legionaries called the pits lilies.
These are not soldiers who can dig.
They are engineers who happen to fight.

recordings.transcript: The riders begin to work. A relief army is coming — tribes converging from across Gaul. Caesar's answer is to build the whole thing again, facing the other way. Twenty-one more kilometres, a complete second ring enclosing the first. His army now holds a corridor between two walls, besieging a fortress while itself besieged. Caesar writes that a quarter of a million men are marching toward him. Historians think far fewer. More, certainly, than he could meet in the open.

recordings.transcript: The food inside runs out first. Vercingetorix expels the Mandubii — the people whose town it is, the ones not fighting. Women, children and the old walk down to the Roman lines and ask to be let through. Caesar refuses. They cannot go back up and they cannot come forward, so they stay in the open ground between the walls, where both armies can see them, and starve. Caesar records this in one sentence and moves on.

Vercingetorix expels the Mandubii — the people whose town it is, the ones not fighting.
Women, children and the old walk down to the Roman lines and ask to be let through.
Caesar refuses.
They cannot go back up and they cannot come forward, so they stay in the open ground between the walls, where both armies can see them, and starve.
Caesar records this in one sentence and moves on.

recordings.transcript: The relief force arrives and attacks both walls at once. Vercassivellaunus finds the single place the fortifications could not follow the ground — a slope on the northwest where the line runs wrong — and throws sixty thousand men at it. Labienus is sent with what can be spared. Caesar takes cavalry out through his own lines and comes around behind the attackers, in a red cloak, deliberately visible, so that both armies know exactly where he is.

recordings.transcript: The relief army breaks and scatters in the night. The next morning Vercingetorix surrenders. Caesar gives it one flat sentence. Plutarch, writing a century and a half later, adds the full armour, the circle on horseback, the weapons laid at Caesar's feet. Vercingetorix is kept alive in a Roman cell for six years, walked through Rome in Caesar's triumph, and strangled.
